positions.claim: AI models generate security issues in code just as human developers do, so this is not a novel or especially alarming risk.
Security must be a core part of the modern development lifecycle regardless of whether code is written by humans or AI.
Safely deploying autonomous agents into production is a substantially harder problem than securing AI-generated code.
Geopolitics — specifically restricted access to frontier models like Fable and GPT-5.6 — is now a real barrier to innovation and speed for AI engineers.
Model access restrictions are fundamentally a security problem, not merely a policy or commercial one.
The biggest remaining unsolved problem in AI engineering is being able to use AI fearlessly with security by default.
Generative AI's primary value to engineers is shipping higher-quality software to users faster, rather than any other capability.
Manual human-in-the-loop agent iteration stops scaling once an organization runs a large number of agents or AI features, making agentic automation of the loop necessary.
The agent spec should be kept independent of the implementation framework, because teams will likely need to switch harnesses within roughly a year.
A complete eval suite cannot be written upfront by domain experts; it must be discovered incrementally from production failures and user feedback.
Binary pass/fail eval criteria are preferable to score-based rubrics because they yield actionable, fixable feedback.
Uncalibrated LLM judges produce enough run-to-run variance that you cannot conclusively compare agent versions.
Agents must be evaluated across the full trajectory — context completeness, every tool output, and the harness — not on final output alone.
At millions of traces, reading all traces with an LLM costs more than the original agent executions, so representative sampling with learned indicators is required.
If an optimized agent variant meets target eval scores, it can be shipped to production automatically without human review.
The harness an agent runs on is itself a legitimate optimization variable, alongside prompts and tools.
Automated diagnostics reports must surface their assumptions explicitly, because agents reading traces without code access will infer things that are wrong.
The system that generates code must not be the same system that validates it.
AI-generated code quality is measurably worse than human-generated code from a security standpoint.
Enterprise vulnerability backlogs grew 108% quarter over quarter across 4,800+ customers in the past year.
Severity-based triage (fixing only criticals and highs) is no longer defensible because agents can chain low-severity vulnerabilities into working exploits.
More than a third of publicly shared agent skills contain malware or vulnerabilities.
MCP is a good protocol but shipped with very little security built in.
Repositories contain roughly three times more agentic components (agents, tools) than models, so risk assessment must span all layers.
Latest frontier models find the same vulnerability in only 50% of five repeated runs, detect 75% of issues relative to a deterministic check, and score 40% F1.
Waiting for a better model to solve agentic security is the wrong strategy.
Model safety properties are not monotonic — a model can be perfectly resistant to decision override while being 100% vulnerable to PII extraction, so model selection must be per-use-case.
AI governance expressed as documentation (Confluence pages, PDFs) is ineffective; it must be enforced in real time in the agent and developer loop.
Package selection should weigh maintenance health, not just current CVE count, because unmaintained packages get patched slower when new vulnerabilities appear.
Security tooling should be invoked deterministically via hooks or skills rather than relying on the developer to prompt for it.
AI does have a legitimate role in security — an agent remediated 16,000 critical issues at one large company — the point is scoping it to what it does well.
